Here is what I have been focusing on lately...trying to combine multiple concepts in to a workable trade setup that can be repeated.

I am finding the best IQM levels are a result of an important FL being FO...the more important the FL, the more important the IQM bounce. For example, some of the best bounces occur after an engulf of an ORFL.

These don't always work..but they usually give at least a mild bounce.

I think the success of this setup (and others like it) really depends on the FO. These trades all react around a trick being played...so it makes logical sense that focusing on the nastiest tricks will give us a hint as to the location for a strong future reaction.

This got me thinking...what constitutes a nasty trick? To me, it is a trick that pulls in the most number of victims...I want the really obvious tricks.

I ask:

1. Where on the chart will the herd be trading the most? 2. What trade is the herd looking for?

author: hoeschec
text:
I have been pondering a new theory lately...nothing too spectacular...just been experimenting with session highs/lows. I know this strays away from the core RTM strategy, so if this is too off topic please let me know and I will delete the post.

I think session highs/lows are important to consider. Not because they hold significance based on theory...but they hold significance because many traders think of them as being important. They have all kinds of indicators that trade based on a break of a previous sessions high/low. Breakout traders love these trades..especially if the session high/low happens at round number. We want to trade where the herd's stop losses are located.

It makes logical sense to choose areas on the chart where the highest number of traders are likely to get caught on the wrong side of the trade.

What better place to look than at a FO of a session high or low? So many traders would get in on the breakout and get caught on the FO.

Here is an example: EUR-USD:

Red shading is NY green is London

1. LS that holds as the high of both the London AND NY Session. 2. LTF shows this as the first break and retest of the LS. This is the LS Kink.

3. The break above # 1 is a false break and many traders are caught trying to unload long positions. This is a RBD FO. 4. Price drops considerably making a new low 5. Price works its way back to the old Kink and there is a nice reaction that occurs at the FTR.

Note the downside engulf that forms just before the spike @ # 5

Here is another example on USD-CHF: same 1-5 labels.

author: hoeschec
text:
In reference to my previous post (post # 1696)

I am trying to filter out weaker trade opps by thinking about "why" price reacts the way it does at certain levels.

It reminds me of high school math.

You can take and pass a calculus course relatively easily...by simply memorizing how to solve math problems. Math is systematic...it is exact and the process to solve the problems are well-defined and consistent. You can get an A in calculus by memorizing the steps. The harder part is understanding why...the application is the hard part.

So in terms of trading, I want to think about why price moves the way it does. Not just memorize terms and abbreviations and boxes. But understand the context behind what all of this means.

Price capping out at the London and NY session high is a good place to look for a FO but it isn't the only place. Any area of the charts where the herd is caught on the wrong side of a trade is a good place to look for a bounce/reaction.
